tour.launch: take a tour of the stage
tour.stage: The /stage/ shows your program's *current value*. That value might be a *raw value* like a number or list, *visual output* you can see, or even *sound* you can hear.
tour.reset: The /reset/ button starts your program's evaluation over from the *beginning*, in any mode: in ▶️ *play* it performs again from the top, in ✏️ *edit* it pauses after the first evaluation so you can see your edits' effect on the initial output, and in ⏸️ *debug* it pauses at the very first step.
tour.zoom: The /zoom/ buttons let you zoom *in* and *out* on the stage so you can see your output more clearly or in greater detail.
tour.grid: The /grid/ button shows a *grid* on the stage, helpful for placing things precisely while you design.
tour.lock: The /lock/ button locks the stage's view in place. When *locked*, the stage stays still; when *unlocked*, you can pan and zoom freely.
tour.animationSpeed: The /animation speed/ control sets how fast animations play. The same control is in *settings*, so you can change it from either place.

tour.timeline: The /timeline/ lets you step *forward* and *backward* through your program's evaluation, one step at a time. It appears in the stage's toolbar in ✏️ *edit* and ⏸️ *debug* modes, and it's a great way to see *how* your program computes its value, and to build a mental model of how @wordplay programs evaluate, especially if you're not seeing the behavior you want.
tour.modes: The /mode switcher/ chooses how your program evaluates. In ✏️ *edit* mode, the program pauses wherever it is and you can change it — your edits replay to show their effect at that point. In ⏸️ *debug* mode, the code is read-only and the *current value* of each part of your program appears next to it in the editor and in the palette. In ▶️ *play* mode, your program runs live from where it is, responding to inputs in real time. Beside the switcher, the /perform/ button — a play triangle wrapped in full screen corners — begins a performance from the top and fills the screen with the stage, and ↻ resets the program in any mode.
tour.annotations: The /annotations/ window is where explanations of each step appear. As you step through your program, this is where you'll read what just happened.
tour.editor: The /editor/ shows your code. While stepping, the *value* of each part of your program will appear next to that part *after* it's been evaluated, so you can watch values build up as the program runs.
tour.history: The /history/ shows every *input* your program has received, like keys, time ticks, and pointer events. It's *draggable*, so you can return to any moment in the program's evaluation history just by dragging. If you'd rather *hear* those inputs than see them, turn on /evaluation cues/ in settings, and @wordplay will play a short sound for each one, with a different sound for each kind of input.
tour.stepControls: The /step controls/ let you move through evaluation precisely. You can jump to the *start* or *end*, step *forward* or *backward* one step at a time, jump by *one input*, step *out* of a function, or jump to the *currently selected* part of the code.

share.explanation: Share this project with galleries or the world.

gallery.explanation: Add this project in a gallery alongside other creators, or create a gallery on your <projects@://projects> page. If you add a project to a public gallery, your project will become public.

public.explanation: Public projects and galleries can be seen by anyone in the world. Our goal is for this content to bring affirmation and joy, and publicly sharing is a way to do that. But it also means following some rules. You promise that your project does not:

pii.explanation:
Sharing personally identifiable information (PII) publicly can put creators at risk, so we detect possible PII and warn creators to either remove the sensitive data or mark it as non-sensitive.

Below is a list of possible PII in this project you have marked as non-sensitive. You can click the button next to it to mark it as sensitive again, but doing so means that your project won't be saved online anymore.

preview.explanation: This is the little glyph that represents your project in lists and galleries. Auto picks one based on what your project shows; Custom lets you pin a single character or emoji.

remix.explanation: A /remix/ is a copy of a project that someone changed to make their own. We remember where a remix came from, so the person who made the original still gets credit.

research.explanation:
Sometimes we write and talk about Wordplay — in research papers, in talks, and in what we show teachers and families. If you turn this on, we can show this project as an example, without your name, your username, or anything else that says the account is yours.

You can turn this off any time. Turning it off means we stop using your project in anything new, but it can't take back something we already published or presented.

kit.explanation: A kit is one source you've published for other people to build with. Anything you mark with ↑ becomes part of it.

tour.collaborate: Everyone who can reach this project is listed here, and you can *chat* with the people who are allowed to. Only the /owner/, /collaborators/, and /commenters/ can see the chat.
tour.collaborators: Each person has one /privilege/. *Collaborate* means they can edit the project and chat about it. *Comment* means they can chat but not edit. *View* means they can look but not chat. *Owner* hands them the project. A gallery's /curators/ can always reach it, so you cannot change theirs.
tour.add: Press the *+* at the end of the list to add someone. Type their *email* or *username*, choose what they can do, and they'll join the list.
tour.restrict: When a project is in a *gallery*, by default *everyone* who can see the gallery can see your project. The /restrict/ toggle *hides* it from everyone except you and the gallery curators.

presence.waitingForSlot: Waiting for an editing slot — four collaborators are already editing. When one leaves, you'll be able to edit too.

tour.launch: take a tour of the palette
tour.palette: You can use the /palette/ to edit *phrases*, *groups*, and the *stage* in ✏️ *edit* mode; in other modes its controls are read-only, and in ⏸️ *debug* mode each property also shows its *current value*.
tour.text: All the /properties/ of a phrase can be edited here. This is the *text* of the phrase, but other properties have their own controls.
tour.set: When a property is currently using its /default/ value, the *pencil* button lets you set an *explicit* value for it.
tour.unset: When a property has an /explicit/ value set, the *X* button removes that value, returning the property to its *default*.
tour.editor: All of the changes you make in the palette are reflected in the /code/ shown in the *editor*.
tour.stage: Phrases can also be /moved/, /resized/, and /rotated/ directly on the *stage*.

localize.guidanceEmpty: No guidance yet. Write what someone translating into this language should know.

terms.description: Define terms and phrases for this language that you can reuse anywhere by writing $$ and the word's key, like $$program. When you change a word here, it changes everywhere it's used, so your translations stay consistent. This is just for reusing words; to explain a term to learners, use the glossary instead.
terms.empty: No words yet. Add one to reuse it across this language's text.

key.description: the key for this word, written after a $ to use it

phrase.description: the word or phrase this key stands for

terms.add: add this word to the list
terms.remove: remove this word from the list
terms.invalidKey: A key must start with a letter and use only letters and numbers, in any language.
terms.duplicateKey: This language already has a word with that key.
terms.reservedKey: That key is already used for a template value, so it can't be a word.

glossary.description: The glossary explains words learners meet. Each term has one main word, and here you can add the other ways that word gets written in this language — plurals, other endings, or another word that means the same. When writing text, you can link any of them with @ and the word, and the whole word stays part of the link. Every language writes its own list, so add as many or as few as your language needs.

form.description: another way this term is written

glossary.add: add this form to the term

glossary.conceptName: The documentation already defines this word, so a link to it would go there instead.
glossary.alreadyUsed: This is already a form of $term, so it would be unclear which term you meant.
glossary.searchOnly: A link ends at a space or a symbol, so this form will only help searching.
